question: What must a multi-engine Class B aeroplane show at take-off, beyond the single-engine requirements?

options.text: An accelerate-stop distance within ASDA on every runway

explanation: Multi-engine Class B aeroplanes (other than commuter) have the same field length rules as singles, plus climb gradient and obstacle clearance requirements.

question: When several climb gradient requirements apply, which decides the maximum permissible mass?

options.text: The average of all of them

explanation: Three climb requirements are checked; the most limiting determines the maximum mass.

question: What all-engines climb gradient is required of a multi-engine Class B aeroplane after take-off?
explanation: With all engines at take-off power, flaps at take-off and the specified speed, the climb gradient must be at least 4%.

question: For the 4% all-engines climb requirement, when may the gear be assumed retracted?

options.text: When it retracts in 7 seconds or less
When it retracts in 15 seconds or less

explanation: The gear is assumed extended, unless it can be retracted in not more than 7 seconds, when it may be assumed retracted.

question: What climb speed applies to the 4% all-engines requirement?

options.text: The speed achieved at the 50 ft screen height

explanation: The all-engines climb speed must be at least the greater of 1.1 VMC and 1.2 VS1.

question: What one-engine-inoperative gradient is required at 400 ft above the take-off surface?
explanation: At 400 ft, with the critical engine inoperative and its propeller in the minimum drag position, gear up, take-off flap and the 50 ft speed, the gradient must be measurably positive.

question: For the 400 ft one-engine-inoperative requirement, in what configuration is the aeroplane?

options.text: Gear extended, flaps in the take-off position
Gear retracted, flaps in the take-off position

explanation: At 400 ft the gear is up, flaps are at the take-off setting, the live engine at take-off power, and the speed as at 50 ft.

question: What one-engine-inoperative gradient is required at 1 500 ft above the take-off surface?
explanation: At 1 500 ft, with the critical engine inoperative, the live engine at no more than MCP, gear and flaps up and at least 1.2 VS1, the gradient must be at least 0.75%.

question: For the 1 500 ft one-engine-inoperative requirement, what power is used on the live engine?
explanation: At 1 500 ft the live engine is at not more than maximum continuous power, with flaps and gear retracted.

question: In the one-engine-inoperative climb requirements, where is the failed engine's propeller assumed to be?

options.text: Windmilling in fine pitch at take-off rpm

explanation: The critical engine is inoperative with its propeller in the minimum drag (feathered) position.

question: For a multi-engine Class B aeroplane, which field length rules apply?

options.text: TOD × 1.15 must not exceed TORA only
The Class A rules, using a balanced field length

explanation: The field length requirements are identical: TOD × 1.25 ≤ TORA without stopway or clearway; with them, TOD ≤ TORA, × 1.3 ≤ ASDA and × 1.15 ≤ TODA.

question: What two kinds of take-off chart are typically provided for a light twin?
explanation: Light twins usually have a normal take-off chart and a maximum-effort or short-field chart, each with its own speeds.

question: Is an accelerate-stop distance requirement applied to a multi-engine Class B aeroplane (not commuter)?

options.text: Yes, but only on wet runways
No, although the data may be given
Yes, ASD × 1.3 must not exceed ASDA
Yes, ASD must not exceed TORA

explanation: Other than for commuter category aeroplanes there is no accelerate-stop requirement, though the manual may give the data.

question: For a commuter category aeroplane, which three parts make up the accelerate-stop distance?

options.text: Accelerate to VR, then stop from VR
Accelerate to V2, then stop from V2
Accelerate to VEF, accelerate from VEF to V1, then stop
Accelerate to V1, rotate, then stop from the rotation speed

explanation: ASD = all-engines acceleration to VEF, acceleration from VEF to V1 with the critical engine failed, and a full stop from V1.

question: For a multi-engine Class B aeroplane, what is the minimum rotation speed VR?

options.text: The greater of 1.1 VMC and 1.2 VS1
The greater of 1.05 VMC and 1.1 VS1

explanation: VR must be no less than 1.05 VMC and no less than 1.1 VS1.

question: For a multi-engine Class B aeroplane, what is the minimum speed at the 50 ft screen?

options.text: The greater of 1.05 VMC and 1.1 VS1

explanation: The take-off safety speed must be no less than a speed safe under all reasonable conditions, 1.1 VMC and 1.2 VS1.

question: VMC is 70 kt and VS1 is 65 kt. What is the minimum VR for a light twin?
explanation: 1.05 × 70 = 73.5 kt; 1.1 × 65 = 71.5 kt. The greater, 73.5 kt, is the minimum VR.

question: VMC is 70 kt and VS1 is 65 kt. What is the minimum speed at 50 ft for a light twin?
explanation: 1.1 × 70 = 77 kt; 1.2 × 65 = 78 kt. The greater, 78 kt, is the minimum (unless a higher safe speed is needed).

question: For take-off, what is the maximum value VMC may have for a light twin?
explanation: VMC for take-off must not exceed 1.2 VS1.

question: Up to what height must a multi-engine Class B aeroplane show obstacle clearance after take-off?
explanation: Multi-engine Class B aeroplanes must demonstrate clearance of obstacles from 50 ft up to 1 500 ft above the surface.

question: What vertical obstacle clearance must a multi-engine Class B aeroplane achieve?
explanation: Obstacles must be cleared by a vertical margin of at least 50 ft, or by the specified horizontal distance.

question: What horizontal obstacle clearance is required, where D is the distance from the end of the TODA?
explanation: The horizontal margin is at least 90 m + 0.125 D. For aeroplanes with a wingspan under 60 m it may be 60 m + half the wingspan + 0.125 D.

question: From where is D measured in the horizontal clearance formula if a turn is scheduled before the end of the TODA?

options.text: From the end of the TORA
From the end of the TOD

explanation: D is the distance from the end of the TODA, or from the end of the TOD if a turn is scheduled before the end of the TODA.

question: An obstacle is 2 000 m from the end of the TODA. What horizontal clearance is required (standard formula)?
An aeroplane with a 12 m wingspan passes an obstacle 2 000 m from the end of the TODA. Using the small-wingspan formula, what horizontal clearance is required?
Where is the take-off flight path for obstacle clearance assumed to begin and end?

options.text: At brake release, ending at 400 ft
From 50 ft at TODR end to 1 500 ft
From lift-off at VLOF, ending at 3 000 ft above the runway

explanation: The path starts 50 ft above the surface at the end of the take-off distance required and ends 1 500 ft above the surface.

question: What bank angle limits are assumed in the take-off flight path?

options.text: No bank below 35 ft; then no more than 30°
No bank below 400 ft; then no more than 25°
No bank below 50 ft; then no more than 15°

explanation: The aeroplane is not banked before 50 ft, and thereafter the bank does not exceed 15°.

question: Where is the critical engine assumed to fail in the multi-engine Class B obstacle calculation?

options.text: At the screen height of 50 ft

explanation: The failure is assumed at the point on the all-engines path where visual reference for avoiding obstacles is expected to be lost, for example at the cloud base.

question: Which gradient is assumed from 50 ft to the point of engine failure?

options.text: The all-engines average gradient reduced by 0.5%

explanation: The all-engines net gradient is the average all-engines gradient during climb and transition, multiplied by 0.77.

question: Which gradient is assumed from the point of engine failure up to 1 500 ft?
explanation: From the failure point to 1 500 ft, the one-engine-inoperative (en route) gross gradient is assumed.

question: The flight path needs no track change of more than 15°, in VMC. Beyond what lateral distance need obstacles not be considered?
explanation: With track changes up to 15°, obstacles further than 300 m laterally in VMC, or 600 m otherwise, need not be considered.

question: The flight path needs a track change of more than 15°, not in VMC. Beyond what lateral distance need obstacles not be considered?
explanation: With track changes over 15°, the limits are 600 m in VMC and 900 m in other conditions.

question: Which of these must the take-off flight path calculation account for?

options.text: Number of passengers and the type of fuel loaded

explanation: The flight path takes account of the mass at the start of the take-off run, pressure altitude, ambient temperature, and not more than 50% headwind or not less than 150% tailwind.

question: The all-engines gross gradient is 10%. What net gradient is used for obstacle clearance before engine failure?
explanation: Net gradient = gross gradient × 0.77 = 7.7%.

question: Visibility is clear to 1 500 ft. With an all-engines net gradient of 7.7%, what distance is needed from 50 ft to 1 500 ft?
explanation: Height gain = 1 450 ft; 1 450 ÷ 7.7 × 100 ≈ 18 830 ft. Using 1 500 ft gives 19 480 ft.

question: With an all-engines net gradient of 7.7%, an obstacle 600 ft high lies 8 000 ft beyond reference zero. Is it cleared by the required margin?

options.text: No, the aeroplane is below it

explanation: Height = 8 000 × 0.077 + 50 = 616 + 50 = 666 ft; clearance 66 ft, more than the 50 ft required.

question: If the 50 ft obstacle clearance is not achieved, what is done?

options.text: The net gradient is increased by 0.5%
A lower mass is assumed and the path recalculated
The aeroplane departs anyway in VMC

explanation: A lower take-off mass is assumed, a new height at the obstacle found, and the mass that just clears by 50 ft found by interpolation.

question: The cloud base is 800 ft. With an all-engines net gradient of 7.7%, how far is it from 50 ft to the cloud base?
Continuing from an 800 ft cloud base, the one-engine-inoperative gross gradient is 2%. How far is it from the cloud base to 1 500 ft?
How is a rate of climb converted to a gradient?

options.text: Ground speed ÷ rate of climb × 100, in feet per minute

explanation: Gradient % = rate of climb (ft/min) ÷ true ground speed (ft/min) × 100.

question: A twin climbs at 400 ft/min with a ground speed of 120 kt. What is its gradient?
A twin climbs 700 ft at 350 ft/min with a ground speed of 6 000 ft/min. What ground distance is covered?
explanation: Time = 700 ÷ 350 = 2 min; distance = 6 000 × 2 = 12 000 ft.
